title: Crimes Act 1914 (Cth) - Full Text
text:
Spent convictions legislation in Australia allows certain criminal convictions to become "spent" after a qualifying period, meaning they no longer need to be disclosed in most circumstances. The primary federal legislation governing spent convictions is Part VIIC of the Crimes Act 1914 (Commonwealth).

Under the Commonwealth scheme, a conviction becomes spent after a waiting period of 10 years for adults (or 5 years for juvenile offenders), provided the person has not reoffended during that period. Once spent, the conviction generally cannot be disclosed on a police check result and employers cannot require the person to disclose it.

However, the spent convictions scheme has significant exclusions. Convictions resulting in a prison sentence of more than 30 months cannot become spent under Commonwealth law. Sexual offences against children are also permanently excluded from the scheme in most jurisdictions. Certain regulated industries — including positions involving children, aged care, and national security — may be exempt from the spent convictions scheme, meaning all convictions remain disclosable regardless of the waiting period.

Each state and territory has its own spent convictions legislation, and the rules differ. For example, Victoria's Spent Convictions Act 2021 allows some sentences exceeding the Commonwealth threshold to become spent. Queensland's Criminal Law (Rehabilitation of Offenders) Act 1986 has a rehabilitation period of 10 years. New South Wales uses the Criminal Records Act 1991, which provides for a 10-year conviction-free period for adults.

For employers, the practical implications are significant. When a police check returns a result, the employer should only see disclosable convictions — not spent ones. However, employers in exempt categories (childcare, aged care, law enforcement) may receive more comprehensive disclosures. Employers must understand which category their roles fall under and apply the correct assessment framework.

Key employer obligations include not asking applicants to disclose spent convictions (unless in an exempt category), not using spent conviction information in hiring decisions even if inadvertently disclosed, and maintaining policies that align with anti-discrimination legislation. The Australian Human Rights Commission provides guidance on managing criminal history in employment decisions.

Validex police checks are processed through the ACIC's National Police Checking Service, which applies the relevant spent convictions legislation automatically, ensuring that only disclosable information is included in results.

title: Services Australia - Identity Confirmation (100-Point)
text:
Identity verification is a critical step in the Australian police check application process. The system used by most accredited bodies follows a points-based model, commonly referred to as the 100-point identity check, to confirm that the applicant is who they claim to be.

The 100-point system assigns point values to different categories of identity documents. Applicants must present documents totalling at least 100 points from specified categories. The three main categories are commencement of identity documents, primary documents, and secondary documents.

Commencement of identity documents establish the basis of the applicant's identity in Australia. These include an Australian birth certificate, Australian citizenship certificate, or a current passport (Australian or foreign). A commencement document is typically worth 70 points and is mandatory for all applications.

Primary documents are government-issued documents that confirm identity and are commonly used in the community. These include a current Australian driver licence, a current Australian passport, a Medicare card, or a current proof of age card. Primary documents are generally worth 40 points each.

Secondary documents provide supporting evidence of identity. These include utility bills, bank statements, a current lease agreement, an Australian tax assessment notice, or a current student ID card. Secondary documents are usually worth 25 points each.

For online police check applications through providers like Validex, identity verification increasingly uses digital verification technology. This involves capturing images of identity documents, extracting data using optical character recognition (OCR), and performing a live selfie comparison using facial recognition. Digital verification can be completed in minutes and provides a higher level of assurance than manual document review.

Common mistakes that cause identity verification failures include providing expired documents, using documents with different name spellings, submitting poor quality images or scans, and not providing a commencement document. Applicants who have changed their name must provide evidence of the name change, such as a marriage certificate or change of name certificate.

For applicants who cannot complete digital verification — for example, if they do not have a suitable device or their documents cannot be read digitally — alternative manual verification pathways are available, though these typically extend processing times.

Employers should clearly communicate identity requirements to applicants before they begin the police check process. Providing a checklist of acceptable documents, along with guidance on image quality and name consistency, can significantly reduce verification failures and resubmissions.

title: Home Affairs - VEVO Check Conditions
text:
Right to work verification is a critical pre-employment check for all Australian employers. Under the Migration Act 1958, it is an offence for an employer to knowingly or recklessly allow a non-citizen to work in Australia without a valid visa that permits work. Penalties for non-compliance are significant and can include fines and criminal prosecution.

The Visa Entitlement Verification Online (VEVO) system is the primary tool for employers to verify a person's visa status and work rights. VEVO is a free service provided by the Department of Home Affairs that allows employers to check whether a visa holder is entitled to work in Australia, the conditions attached to their visa, and the expiry date of their visa.

Employers can access VEVO through the Department of Home Affairs website or through integrated HR systems. To perform a check, the employer needs the person's date of birth and either their passport details, ImmiCard number, or visa grant number. The VEVO result confirms the visa subclass, work entitlements, and any conditions (such as work hour limitations for student visa holders).

Common visa categories relevant to employment screening include Subclass 482 (Temporary Skill Shortage), Subclass 500 (Student Visa — limited to 48 hours per fortnight during study periods), Subclass 485 (Temporary Graduate), Subclass 820/801 (Partner Visa), and Subclass 189/190 (Skilled Permanent Visa — unrestricted work rights).

Employers should perform VEVO checks before the employee commences work and at regular intervals for temporary visa holders, particularly before each visa expiry date. Many employers set calendar reminders or use HR systems to automate visa expiry tracking.

For police check applications, immigration status affects the scope of the check. Non-citizens may require an international police check from their country of origin in addition to an Australian police check, depending on how long they have resided in Australia. Generally, if a person has lived in Australia for less than 12 months continuously, an overseas check may be appropriate.

New Zealand citizens working in Australia under the Trans-Tasman Travel Arrangement have special arrangements. They can live and work in Australia indefinitely on a Special Category Visa (Subclass 444) but may need to apply for a police check through the Australian system.

Validex supports right to work compliance by integrating police check applications with guidance on additional screening requirements based on the applicant's visa status and country of origin.

title: Fair Work - Visa Holders and Migrants
text:
Employer compliance in background screening requires a structured approach to consent, processing, decision-making, record retention, and ongoing governance. Australian employers have legal obligations under privacy law, anti-discrimination law, and industry-specific regulations when conducting police checks and other background screening.

Consent is the foundation of lawful screening. Before initiating a police check, the employer must obtain the applicant's informed, written consent. The consent form should clearly state the purpose of the check, what information will be obtained, who will have access to the results, and how long the information will be retained. Under the Privacy Act 1988, personal information collected for screening purposes must only be used for that purpose.

When a police check returns a disclosable result (a non-clean outcome), the employer must follow a fair assessment process. This means evaluating the relevance of the disclosed information to the specific role. Key factors to consider include the nature of the offence, how long ago it occurred, the applicant's age at the time, the applicant's conduct since the offence, and the specific duties and risk profile of the role.

Employers should not adopt blanket policies that automatically exclude applicants with any criminal history. The Australian Human Rights Commission advises that criminal record discrimination may constitute unlawful discrimination under federal and state anti-discrimination legislation. Each case should be assessed individually based on the inherent requirements of the role.

Record retention obligations require employers to store screening results securely and for no longer than necessary. Industry guidelines recommend retaining police check results for no more than 12 months unless a longer period is required by law or regulation. Access to screening results should be restricted to authorised personnel only — typically the HR compliance officer or designated decision-maker.

Ongoing governance includes conducting periodic audits of screening practices, updating screening policies when legislation changes, training hiring managers on lawful assessment procedures, and maintaining a register of all checks conducted. Employers in regulated industries (childcare, aged care, healthcare, financial services) should review their screening requirements annually.

For organisations using Validex, compliance is supported through automated consent collection, secure result delivery, audit trail maintenance, and integration with HR systems to track screening status across the workforce.

title: NSW - Working With Children Check (OCG)
text:
Working With Children Check (WWCC) is a mandatory screening requirement across all Australian states and territories for individuals who work or volunteer with children. Each jurisdiction administers its own WWCC scheme, though the purpose is consistent: to assess whether a person poses a risk to the safety of children based on their criminal history and other relevant records.

In New South Wales, the WWCC is managed by the Office of the Children's Guardian. Applicants apply online, provide identity verification, and receive either a clearance or a bar. A WWCC clearance in NSW is valid for five years and must be verified by the employer through the online system. Paid workers pay a fee, while volunteers can apply at no cost.

In Victoria, the Working with Children Check is administered by the Department of Justice and Community Safety. A valid Victorian WWCC card is required before commencing child-related work. The card is valid for five years and is linked to the cardholder's criminal record, meaning it can be revoked at any time if new relevant information is recorded.

In Queensland, the Blue Card system serves as the equivalent of the WWCC. Managed by Blue Card Services, it screens individuals working in regulated child-related activities. Processing times vary, but most applications are assessed within four to six weeks. A Blue Card must be renewed before it expires.

Key differences between states include the application fee structure, whether volunteers are exempt, renewal periods, and which offences are classified as disqualifying. Employers must verify that a worker holds a valid WWCC before they begin child-related duties, and must notify the relevant authority if the worker's role changes or if they become aware of relevant criminal charges.

Failure to hold a valid WWCC when required is a criminal offence in most jurisdictions. Employers who knowingly engage an unscreened worker may also face penalties. For organisations operating across multiple states, managing WWCC compliance requires awareness of each jurisdiction's rules and renewal timelines.

Validex supports WWCC compliance by providing guidance on which checks are needed for specific roles and helping employers track screening status across their workforce.

title: Aged Care Quality - Worker Screening
text:
Aged care worker screening in Australia is governed by the Aged Care Act 1997 and its associated regulations. All workers in Commonwealth-funded aged care services must undergo a police check before commencing work and at regular intervals thereafter. This requirement was strengthened following the recommendations of the Royal Commission into Aged Care Quality and Safety.

The Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission (ACQSC) oversees compliance with screening requirements for approved providers. Under current legislation, a person is not eligible to work in aged care if they have been convicted of murder or sexual assault. For other offences, the provider must conduct a risk assessment to determine whether the person is suitable for the role.

Police checks for aged care workers are typically required every three years, although some providers implement annual screening as a matter of best practice. The check must be obtained through an ACIC-accredited body and must be a nationally coordinated criminal history check.

In addition to police checks, aged care workers in certain states may also require an NDIS Worker Screening Check if the service provides supports to NDIS participants. This dual requirement means that aged care providers must track both police check validity and NDIS screening status for relevant workers.

Key responsibilities for aged care providers include maintaining a register of all workers and their screening status, ensuring new workers are screened before their first shift with residents, conducting risk assessments for workers with disclosable criminal history, implementing policies for managing workers whose checks are pending or have returned adverse results, and notifying the ACQSC of any reportable incidents related to worker conduct.

The Serious Incident Response Scheme (SIRS) requires aged care providers to report and manage serious incidents, including allegations of criminal conduct by workers. A robust screening program helps prevent such incidents by identifying potential risks before workers commence in roles with vulnerable people.

For workers who hold a current police check from another industry (such as childcare or healthcare), the aged care provider should verify whether the check meets the specific requirements of the aged care sector. Generally, a police check obtained for another purpose is acceptable if it is a nationally coordinated check and is within the provider's accepted validity period.

Validex provides police checks that meet the requirements of the aged care sector, with processing typically completed within one to three business days. Employers can use the Validex platform to manage bulk screening requests and track compliance across their workforce.

title: NDIS Commission - Worker Screening
text:
The NDIS Worker Screening Check is a nationally consistent assessment required for workers in certain risk-assessed roles within the National Disability Insurance Scheme. The check is designed to determine whether a person poses an unacceptable risk of harm to people with disability.

NDIS worker screening is administered by each state and territory's worker screening unit. The check assesses a person's national criminal history, relevant disciplinary or misconduct findings, and any other relevant information. The outcome is either a clearance or an exclusion.

Workers in risk-assessed roles — those involving more than incidental contact with NDIS participants — must hold a valid NDIS Worker Screening Check clearance before commencing work. This applies to employees, contractors, and volunteers. Registered NDIS providers are required to ensure all workers in these roles are screened.

The NDIS Worker Screening Check is different from a standard national police check. While a police check reveals disclosable criminal history, the NDIS screening involves a risk assessment that considers how the person's history may affect the safety of people with disability. A person with a criminal history may still receive a clearance if the offences are not relevant to disability support work.

Key aspects of the NDIS Worker Screening Check include continuous monitoring, meaning that once a person is cleared, any subsequent changes to their criminal record are automatically assessed. This is a significant difference from a point-in-time police check.

Processing times vary by jurisdiction but generally take two to four weeks for straightforward applications. Complex cases requiring manual assessment may take longer. Workers can apply through their state or territory's worker screening unit, usually via an online portal.

Employers should maintain a register of all workers who require screening, track clearance expiry dates, and have processes for managing interim arrangements when a worker's check is pending. Validex can assist with tracking screening status and ensuring compliance with NDIS Commission requirements.
